Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day Only indicated, not established: - It is taken as two capsules a day and is listed as NSF Certified for Sport. [1] Only indicated, not established: - Its formula uses L-5-MTHF folate, methylcobalamin B12, P5P B6, bisglycinate minerals. [1] [2] [3] Only indicated, not established: - Per two capsules it has 50 mg thiamin, 20 mg B6 and 2,000 IU vitamin D3. [1] [2] [3] Pure Encapsulations O.N.E. Only indicated, not established: - It is one capsule a day with a meal. [4] [5] Only indicated, not established: - It uses Metafolin folate, methylcobalamin B12, 2,000 IU vitamin D3 and 25 mg zinc citrate. [4] [5] Only indicated, not established: - It also adds CoQ10, alpha-lipoic acid, lutein, zeaxanthin and lycopene. [4] [5] Testing Only indicated, not established: - Pure Encapsulations' own materials say its products are tested by third-party laboratories. [29] [30] [31] [6] [5] [7] - That statement is about the brand, not O.N.E. specifically. I found no NSF Certified for Sport mark for O.N.E (the cited sources do not show: NSF Certified for Sport, O.N.E). [29] [30] [31] [6] [5] [7] - The company also describes its facility as NSF-GMP registered. Only indicated, not established: That is a facility-level credential, not a product mark like Thorne's. [30] Only indicated, not established: - On testing, Thorne has a product-specific sport certification, while Pure Encapsulations has brand-level third-party testing claims. [1] [29] [30] [31] [6] [5] [7] Price - Retail comparisons put O.N.E. cheaper per day than Thorne. Only indicated, not established: The figures differ between sources and change often, so check current prices. [9] [10]
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day is taken as two capsules per day and is listed as NSF Certified for Sport.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Thorne's formula uses L-5-MTHF folate, methylcobalamin B12, P5P B6, bisglycinate minerals and K1 plus MK-4 K2. It has 50 mg thiamin and 20 mg B6 per two capsules, and 2,000 IU vitamin D3.
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: O.N.E. is one capsule daily with a meal. It uses Metafolin folate, methylcobalamin B12, 2,000 IU vitamin D3 and 25 mg zinc citrate. It also adds CoQ10, alpha-lipoic acid, lutein, zeaxanthin and lycopene.

Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Retail price comparisons put O.N.E. cheaper per day than Thorne, but the figures differ between sources and change often.

- Pure Encapsulations' own statement of testing and certifications for O.N.E. — I searched for it and found only retailer and review pages. An NSF Certified for Sport equivalent for O.N.E. was not confirmed.
- Current prices — retail listings conflict and change often. I did not find a price page from either brand.
- Which Thorne and Pure Encapsulations multivitamin variants are current, including the Thorne Multi-Vitamin Elite and Pure's Nutrient 950 line. I compared only t — No source covered it.
- Evidence on health outcomes — I did not look for systematic reviews on whether either product improves health. Nothing here speaks to that.
- Product-specific third-party testing or certificate of analysis for O.N.E. — the one search this call covered the brand's own quality pages. Those state brand-level third-party testing and no O.N.E. certification mark. I did not check the O.N.E. product page itself.
- Dates for c1, c2, c3 and c6 — the pages give no dates, so current accuracy is only indicated. I ran no new search on these this call.
- Current per-day prices (c6) — they change within days and I ran no new search, so no current figures are given.

Thorne or O.N.E. multivitamin for someone avoiding iron — Partly answered: 5 things it rests on aren't established.
I'd pick Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day, but only narrowly. Only indicated, not established: Iron doesn't separate the two, because both are iron-free. Rests on findings that are not established: My pick rests on other things, which I explain below. [36] [37] [38] [1] [39] [40] [20] [41] Only indicated, not established: - Iron: Thorne's two-capsule formula contains no iron. Only indicated, not established: The standard O.N.E. multivitamin is also listed as iron-free. [36] [37] [38] [1] [39] [40] [20] [41] - Wrong-bottle risk: Pure Encapsulations also sells a separate "O.N.E. Multivitamin with Iron" containing iron bisglycinate. Only indicated, not established: Someone avoiding iron should not buy that one. [42] [43] Only indicated, not established: - Why Thorne: It is listed as NSF Certified for Sport. It also includes vitamin K as K1 and MK-4, which O.N.E. lacks (the cited sources do not show: K1 and MK-4). I found no product-specific NSF sport mark for O.N.E (the cited sources do not show: O.N.E). [1] [40] [44] [41] [12] Only indicated, not established: - What O.N.E. offers instead: It is one capsule a day taken with a meal. Only indicated, not established: It also adds CoQ10, alpha-lipoic acid and carotenoids. Not established: It is likely cheaper per day, though the price figures vary by source. [39] [41] [38] I'm assuming the person cares more about third-party sport testing and broader nutrient coverage than about capsule count or price, and that they take no anticoagulant. A choice of O.N.E. over Thorne would make sense if: - they want one capsule a day; - they want CoQ10 and carotenoids; - cost matters most; - they take an anticoagulant such as warfarin, because Thorne contains vitamin K and a retailer page for it warns against use with anticoagulants. [44] [41] [12]
Caveat: Only indicated, not established: Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day contains no iron.

Caveat: Not established: Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day is the narrow pick, because iron does not separate the two products.

Depends on you
- Thorne contains vitamin K1 and MK-4. O.N.E. contains no vitamin K. A retailer page for Thorne cautions against use with anticoagulants. [44] [41] [12]

- Does the person prefer one capsule a day or lower cost over third-party sport testing and vitamin K? That would flip the pick to O.N.E.

What I couldn't establish
- NSF Certified for Sport status of O.N.E. — I searched only O.N.E. supplement facts, not NSF's certification listing, so I can't say whether a sport mark exists.
- Current exact prices — the sources I found disagree, and retail prices change often.

The claim therefore rests on the UK sheet plus agreeing retailer and review p

Recommendation: Pick Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day.
Because: Both are iron-free, so the tie is broken by its NSF Certified for Sport listing and its vitamin K, which O.N.E. lacks (only indicated, not established: Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day contains no iron; only indicated, not established: The standard O.N.E. multivitamin contains no iron; only indicated, not established: Thorne Basic Nutrients 2/Day is marketed as NSF Certified for Sport. Assumes: The person prefers sport-tested quality and fuller nutrient coverage over a single capsule and lower price, and takes no anticoagulant.
